questions.stem: You meet a Japanese exchange student for the first time and want to introduce yourself as Sam.
questions.explanation: 「はじめまして。わたしはサムです。どうぞよろしく。」 (hajimemashite. watashi wa samu desu. douzo yoroshiku.) さん is a courtesy for other people's names, so it is never added to your own. A name is a noun, so it takes です (desu), not a verb ending.

questions.stem: A new classmate asks how old you are, and you are 12.
questions.explanation: 「わたしは十二さいです。」 (watashi wa juunisai desu.) さい (sai) is the counter for years of age; 時 (ji) would make it a clock time and 人 (nin) a number of people. Age is a noun plus です (desu), just as English uses 'am'.

build.translation: I am 12 years old.

questions.stem: Your Japanese pen pal asks where you live. You live in Melbourne.

questions.stem: You are at a counter in Japan and want to order one bowl of ramen.
questions.explanation: 「すみません、ラーメンをひとつください。」 (sumimasen, raamen o hitotsu kudasai.) The thing you want takes を (o), and the number comes after it, before ください (kudasai). つ (tsu) counts things; ひとり, ふたり and にん count people.

questions.stem: A friend asks what you do at weekends. On Saturdays you play tennis in the park.
questions.explanation: 「土よう日にこうえんでテニスをします。」 (doyoubi ni kouen de tenisu o shimasu.) Days of the week take に (ni), the place where you do something takes で (de), and the verb comes last. A habit takes the present ます (masu) form.

build.translation: On Saturdays I play tennis in the park.

questions.stem: A friend asks what you do at weekends. On Sundays you play games at home.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks what you did yesterday. You did your homework at home.
questions.explanation: 「きのううちでしゅくだいをしました。」 (kinou uchi de shukudai o shimashita.) 「きのう」 (kinou) is relative to today, so it takes no に (ni). The place of the action takes で (de), and 'yesterday' needs the past ending ました (mashita).

build.translation: Yesterday I did my homework at home.

questions.stem: A friend asks 「こうえんに行きませんか。」 (kouen ni ikimasen ka.) You want to say yes.

questions.stem: Your host family asks where the cat is. It is under the desk.
questions.explanation: 「ねこはつくえの下にいます。」 (neko wa tsukue no shita ni imasu.) The position word is a noun joined with の (no), and where something is takes に (ni), not で (de). A cat is an animal, so the verb is 「います」.

build.translation: The cat is under the desk.

questions.stem: You are telling a Japanese visitor how you get to school: every day you leave at eight o'clock and go by bus.

questions.stem: Your new classmate asks about your family. You have one older brother.
questions.explanation: 「わたしはあにが一人います。」 (watashi wa ani ga hitori imasu.) Japanese says 'there are' rather than 'I have', so a person takes 「います」 (imasu) and is marked with が (ga). 人 counts people; つ (tsu) counts things.

build.translation: I have one older brother.

questions.stem: Your Japanese teacher asks how many people are in your family. There are 3.
questions.explanation: 「わたしのかぞくは三人です。」 (watashi no kazoku wa sannin desu.) の (no) makes 'my family', かぞく (kazoku) is the topic with は (wa), and 人 (nin) counts people. つ (tsu) would count things and さい (sai) years of age.

build.translation: There are 3 people in my family.

questions.stem: You are telling your Japanese class what you hope to do: next year you want to go to Japan.
questions.explanation: 「らいねん日本に行きたいです。」 (rainen nihon ni ikitai desu.) 「らいねん」 (rainen) takes no に (ni). たいです (tai desu) replaces ます (masu) to mean 'want to', and it goes in place of ます, not after it.

build.translation: Next year I want to go to Japan.
